Context: the previous page reduced the equation for u(x,r) cos(n psi), i.e. u_xx + (1/r)(r u_r)_r - n^2 u/r^2 = 0, to coordinates given by (a+r+xi)/(a-r-xi) = rho e^{i phi}. These are toroidal (bipolar-meridian) coordinates. There Riemann expanded u in cos(m phi) and obtained a hypergeometric-type recursion. This page computes Fourier coefficients and closed forms that feed into that problem.

(A) Cosine expansion of a power of the 'distance' factor (top). The product is (1 - rho e^{i theta})^n (1 - rho e^{-i theta})^n = (1 - 2 rho cos theta + rho^2)^n. Expanding each factor binomially gives sum_m sum_m' (n!)^2 (-1)^{m+m'} rho^{m+m'} e^{(m-m') i theta} / ((n-m)! m! (n-m')! m'!). Riemann puts the two indices as m and s+m. Collecting e^{+-i s theta} gives
(1 - 2 rho cos theta + rho^2)^n = sum_s c_s cos(s theta), with
c_s = 2 sum_{m=0}^{n-s} (n!)^2 (-1)^s rho^{s+2m} / ((n-m)! m! (n-s-m)! (s+m)!) for s >= 1,
and half that for s = 0. Riemann writes the m-sum with the factor cos(theta s) but without the factor 2 (my completion). A struck-through attempt at a closed form follows.

(B) Integral representation. Riemann writes U = int_0^{2pi} f(r cos theta + x i) cos(n theta) d theta. This is a Whittaker/Laplace-type integral, and it solves the equation of the previous page for arbitrary f (my identification of its role). He tries powers (r cos theta + xi + alpha + beta i)^{n+1}; only the cos^n theta terms and higher contribute to cos(n theta). Then he takes the elementary kernel f(t) = 1/(t + c), with c = alpha + beta i, later renamed p + qi.

Substitute y = e^{i theta}, so cos theta = (y + 1/y)/2 and cos(n theta) is replaced by y^{-n} by symmetry. Then
int cos(n theta) d theta / (r cos theta + c) = (2/i) contour-int y^{-n-1} dy / (r(y + 1/y) + 2(xi + p + qi)).
The denominator is proportional to y^2 + 2Py + 1 = (y - alpha)(y - 1/alpha), where P = (p + (x+q) i)/r. Riemann notes 2P = -(alpha + 1/alpha), i.e. alpha + 1/alpha = -2p/r - 2(x+q)i/r. Earlier on the page he writes it with a + sign, an equivalent convention.

The residue at the root inside the unit circle gives (my constant)
int_0^{2pi} cos(n theta) d theta / (r cos theta + c') = (4 pi / r) alpha^n / (alpha - 1/alpha).
Riemann records this as (1/r) alpha^n/(alpha - 1/alpha), also as alpha^n/(1/alpha - alpha) after a choice of root. He also uses alpha - 1/alpha = 2 sqrt(P^2 - 1) = 2 sqrt(P+1) sqrt(P-1), written as (1/r) alpha^n / sqrt(p^2 - 1) with p meaning P.

(C) Real form. Put alpha = rho e^{i phi}. Then
alpha + 1/alpha = (rho + 1/rho) cos phi + i (rho - 1/rho) sin phi,
alpha - 1/alpha = (rho - 1/rho) cos phi + i (rho + 1/rho) sin phi.
Hence Re[alpha^n/(alpha - 1/alpha)] = rho^n [cos(n phi)(rho - 1/rho) cos phi + sin(n phi)(rho + 1/rho) sin phi] / [(rho - 1/rho)^2 cos^2 phi + (rho + 1/rho)^2 sin^2 phi]. This makes the link with the rho, phi coordinates of the previous page.

(D) Higher kernels by differentiating or integrating in p. From alpha + 1/alpha = -2p/r - ..., one gets (alpha - 1/alpha) d alpha/(alpha dp) = -2/r. So
d/dp [alpha^n/(alpha - 1/alpha)] = -(2/r) [n alpha^n/(alpha - 1/alpha)^2 - alpha^n (alpha + 1/alpha)/(alpha - 1/alpha)^3].
This is the coefficient for the kernel 1/(r cos theta + c)^2 and matches the expression written mid-right.
Conversely, integrating alpha^n dp = -(r/2) alpha^n (alpha - 1/alpha) d alpha/alpha gives -(r/2)(alpha^{n+1}/(n+1) - alpha^{n-1}/(n-1)). This is Riemann's r(alpha^{n+1}/(n+1) - alpha^{n-1}/(n-1)), which handles the logarithmic kernel log(r cos theta + c); compare the line log(y - 1/alpha) alpha^n/(1/alpha - alpha).

Purpose: to obtain closed-form particular solutions of the n-th azimuthal Laplace equation, i.e. Fourier coefficients of ring-type potentials, expressed in the alpha = rho e^{i phi} variables. These would then be compared with the series and hypergeometric solutions in toroidal coordinates on the preceding page.
errors: In the cosine expansion of (1-2 rho cos theta + rho^2)^n the factor 2 for s >= 1 is omitted (or the sum is meant over s from -n to n with e^{i s theta}). The range of m (0..n-s) is only sketched.
The constant 4 pi of the residue evaluation is dropped; formulas are recorded only up to a constant factor.
The sign convention for alpha changes: first alpha + 1/alpha = +2(xi+p+qi)/r, later -2p/r - 2(x+q)i/r. The two are equivalent up to alpha -> -alpha, which only changes an overall sign (-1)^{n+1}.
'sqrt(p^2+4)' and 'sqrt(p^2-1)' are written with p standing for P = (p + (x+q)i)/r; p^2+4 appears to be a slip or an unrelated scratch.
'rho^{ns}' is a stray scratch, not part of a derivation.

deep.surprise_reason: Mostly routine contour-integral and Fourier computations. The only mildly notable feature is the use of an integral int f(r cos theta + xi) cos(n theta) d theta as a general solution of the azimuthal Laplace equation, a Whittaker-type representation. Special cases of this go back to Laplace and Jacobi, and Riemann's use of such tools in potential theory is unsurprising.
